summaries.example: Imagine writing: “Dragon has six letters.” You are not talking about a real dragon. You are talking about the word Dragon. Without quotation marks, “Ava likes dragons” talks about a creature or idea. With quotation marks, “Ava” has three letters talks about a name. The marks help language point to language.
summaries.summary: Quotation is a way language can turn toward language. In “Snow is white,” the sentence talks about snow. In “‘Snow is white’ is a sentence,” the quoted words are being discussed. This difference is often called the use–mention distinction: a word is used when it does its ordinary job, and mentioned when we talk about the word itself. Quotation is useful, but it is puzzling. Quotation marks may look like the part doing the pointing, or the expression inside them may be doing it, or the whole combination may work together. Some philosophers even think quotation is not one simple kind of referring. The puzzle becomes clearer when we notice that quoted expressions do not always behave like ordinary words. Replacing a word with another word that means the same thing can change a quoted sentence. We can also make quotations of unfamiliar symbols, and we can understand new quotations without learning each one separately. A full theory should explain these abilities, as well as cases where quoted words are both used to report an idea and mentioned as words someone said.
key_ideas: Quotation lets us talk about language itself.
The same-looking word can do different jobs: it can talk about its usual subject or about the word.
Quotation can refer to new symbols or words that we have never seen before.
Philosophers disagree about exactly what quotation marks do and what quotations refer to.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quotation is part of how we explain language, dictionaries, spelling, grammar, stories, and what people said. It helps us keep track of whether we are talking about a thing or about the words used for that thing. Understanding this difference can prevent confusion in schoolwork and everyday conversation.

important_terms.definition: Using words to talk about the words, letters, or sentences themselves.
Using a word to talk about what it normally stands for, rather than talking about the word itself.
Talking about a word, symbol, or sentence as an object, often by putting it in quotation marks.
A special way of writing or saying something so that it points to an expression, such as a word or sentence.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between “cats are animals” and “Cats has four letters”?
Could people quote something when speaking without visible quotation marks?
When you quote a sentence, are you pointing to its words, its sounds, or its meaning?
Why might two different words with the same meaning not be interchangeable inside quotation marks?

summaries.example: Compare these claims: “Bachelor” has eight letters and “Unmarried man” has eight letters. Even if the two expressions have a similar meaning, the first claim can be true while the second is false, because the quoted expressions have different lengths. This illustrates opacity: inside quotation, replacing an expression with a co-referring or synonymous one need not preserve truth. A more complicated case is mixed quotation: a reporter may say that a scientist described a result as “surprising,” thereby reporting both the scientist’s claim and a word used in the scientist’s wording.
summaries.summary: Quotation is a central metalinguistic device: it allows language to become the topic of language. A sentence such as “‘Aristotle’ refers to Aristotle” contains an expression used to talk about a person and a quoted expression used to talk about a linguistic item. The entry emphasizes that quotation is difficult to characterize. Identifying it by visible marks is incomplete because speech may lack such marks and writing may use italics, boldface, or indentation. Identifying it simply with mention is also controversial, since some theories separate quotation from mention and because the use–mention distinction itself is not theoretically neutral. Theories of quotation ask three main questions: what does the referring, how does it refer, and what sort of entity is its referent? They must also account for several basic features. Quotation is opaque: synonymous or co-referring substitutions may alter truth-value. Variables cannot normally be quantified into quotation. Quotation can introduce unfamiliar symbols and can be understood productively rather than memorized case by case. A quotation has an unusually close connection to the expression it refers to. Mixed quotation adds a dual demand: quoted material can help characterize what someone said while also indicating wording associated with that speaker. The entry surveys competing approaches, including proper-name, description, demonstrative, disquotational, and use/identity theories, without presenting a settled consensus. It also considers whether quotations are ambiguous among types, tokens, shapes, sounds, concepts, and other linguistic or semantic entities, and discusses alternative devices such as token quotes and quasi-quotation.
key_ideas: Quotation is identified uncontroversially through examples, but syntactic and semantic definitions quickly become disputed.

A satisfactory theory must address opacity, the inability to quantify into quotation, quotation of novel symbols, the close relation between a quotation and its referent, productivity, and mixed use and mention.
Major theories disagree about what does the referring: quotation marks, the interior expression, a structured complex, or a speaker’s special use of language.

The disquotational theory emphasizes a simple mapping from a quoted expression to that expression; the demonstrative theory treats quotation as involving demonstration; use-based theories give a central role to quotational use and speaker intentions.
It is disputed whether quotations can refer flexibly to types, tokens, shapes, sounds, concepts, or contents.
Quotation without visible quotation marks, iteration, open quotation, scare quotes, and mixed quotation create further challenges.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quotation affects formal semantics, the philosophy of language, logic, reporting, and ordinary practices such as editing and journalism. It exposes the boundaries between syntax, semantics, and pragmatics: the visible form of a sentence may not by itself settle what is being referred to, while context and speaker intentions may matter. Studying quotation also shows why a small punctuation practice can raise deep questions about reference, compositionality, and how language represents itself.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical distinction between using an expression to talk about its ordinary subject and mentioning the expression as a linguistic object.
A context in which replacing an expression with a synonymous or co-referring expression can change truth-value.
A linguistic device for talking about expressions, such as words, sentences, symbols, or sounds.
The relation between an expression and what it contributes to a sentence’s meaning or reference.
A theory according to which quotation takes an expression as input and returns that expression as its value.
A theory associated with the idea that quotation marks help demonstrate or point to an expression-token.
A form of quotation that reports content while also drawing attention to wording attributed to another speaker.
The ability of a linguistic system to produce and understand indefinitely many new expressions.

questions_to_think_about: Does the use–mention distinction provide a theory of quotation, or does it merely describe an initial intuition?
Why does the failure of substitution inside quotation create a problem for compositional theories?
Can a theory explain how we understand a quotation containing a never-before-seen symbol without treating it as a newly learned name?
Should spoken cases such as introducing oneself by saying one’s name count as quotation without quotation marks?
Does mixed quotation require semantic machinery, pragmatic inference, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose a student writes, “Robot has five letters.” The sentence is not saying that a robot has five letters. It is talking about the word Robot. Now compare “A robot has five letters,” which makes a claim about a kind of machine. The quotation marks change the job of the word. But things get tricky when a reporter writes, “Mina said the test was ‘unfair.’” This can report Mina’s opinion while also pointing to the particular word used in the report.
summaries.summary: Quotation lets us discuss language by making an expression itself the focus. “Birds fly” talks about birds, while “‘Birds fly’ is a sentence” talks about the words or sentence. This is related to the use–mention distinction. Using an expression means employing it in its ordinary role; mentioning it means drawing attention to the expression. The entry warns, however, that this distinction is not as simple as it first appears. Quotation may occur in speech without obvious quotation marks, and writing may use italics or other signals. Also, some philosophers think mentioning and quoting are different things. Several features make quotation philosophically interesting. A quoted expression is opaque: even if another expression has the same meaning or refers to the same thing, replacing it may change the truth of the sentence. We generally cannot place a variable inside quotation and then quantify over what the variable stands for. Quotation can also handle words, letters, and symbols that are new or not part of a language’s usual vocabulary. Speakers can understand and create new quotations, suggesting a productive rule rather than a giant list learned one item at a time. In mixed quotation, a report can communicate what someone meant while also highlighting wording linked to that person. Philosophers propose different explanations. Some treat quotations as special names, some as descriptions built from smaller expressions, some as demonstrations, some as a simple expression-to-expression operation, and some as the result of using language in a special quotational way. Each approach explains some facts well and faces difficulties with others. The entry therefore presents disagreement as a normal part of the subject rather than claiming that one solution has won.
key_ideas: Quotation marks can make a word become the subject of discussion.
It is not settled whether the marks, the words inside them, or the whole construction does the referring.
A quotation does not always act like an ordinary name or phrase.
Similar meanings do not guarantee that two expressions can replace each other inside quotation.
Philosophers test theories by asking how quotation handles new symbols, variables, speech, and reported words.
There is no single agreed-upon theory of quotation.
summaries.why_it_matters: We quote people, titles, instructions, messages, and bits of code all the time. Knowing how quotation works helps us tell apart a person from their name, an idea from the words used to express it, and a report’s meaning from the wording it highlights. Philosophers use these everyday cases to investigate how reference and meaning work.

important_terms.definition: Using language to discuss language, such as talking about a word’s spelling or a sentence’s truth.
Using an expression for what it normally means or names.
Drawing attention to an expression itself rather than only to what it normally means.
A setting where swapping in a similar-meaning expression may change whether a sentence is true.
A view that quotation points to an expression as if it were being shown or demonstrated.
A view that treats quotation as a direct rule: quoting an expression returns that expression.
Quotation that combines reporting an idea with attention to words connected to the speaker’s wording.
A rule or ability that lets speakers understand and create many new expressions.

questions_to_think_about: In “River is a noun,” is River being used or mentioned?
Why does “Bachelor” has eight letters not automatically support “Unmarried man” has eight letters?
Could a quotation refer to a sound or idea instead of written words?
What information is added when a report uses mixed quotation?
Which seems more plausible: quotation as naming, describing, demonstrating, or a special use?
